work_order.understanding: One invariant underlies every finding in this ticket: a schedule_occurrence stamp only means anything next to the schedule link it was minted for. conform() (loot-core/src/server/aql/schema-helpers.ts:134-144) drops a key whose value is undefined and only skips nulls when skipNull is set; convertForInsert (:184) passes { skipNull: true } while convertForUpdate (:187-195) passes no options; db.update() (server/db/index.ts:209-227) emits one sync message per Object.keys(params).filter(k => k !== 'id'). So on UPDATE an omitted field is never written and the column KEEPS its old value, while on INSERT the same omission falls back to column DEFAULT NULL. Seven production client sites send { id, schedule } or { id, schedule: null } and nothing else, so unlinking clears the link and strands the stamp, and relinking pairs that stamp with a schedule it was never minted for — which then blocks BOTH arms of getHasTransactionsQuery (shared/schedules.ts:194-222), so the schedule reads Due when it was in fact paid. batchUpdateTransactions (server/transactions/index.ts:130-138) re-reads every changed row in full before transfer logic runs, so the server cannot distinguish an intentional stamp from an omitted one — which is why the fix belongs on the senders. addTransfer (server/transactions/transfer.ts:61-86) is the server-side instance: it runs the mirror through runRules, accepts a reassigned schedule at :73, writes it to both legs, and derives the occurrence zero times. I re-derived the whole chain from the source rather than accepting it, and ran a standalone tsc probe to settle the one question the previous draft left as a coin-flip, which removed a file from the change.
work_order.root_cause: schedule and schedule_occurrence are written independently on every path that does not pick both off one source, and conform() makes insert and update disagree about what an omitted field means: on UPDATE a dropped key is never written so the stamp is PRESERVED, on INSERT it falls back to the column default NULL. Seven production client sites each hand-roll the same one-field literal, which is why there is no single place to fix the invariant and no existing test that can observe more than one site. addTransfer is the server-side instance: it writes the schedule to two legs and derives the occurrence zero times, so a rule that relinks the transfer leaves both legs stamped for the old schedule.
work_order.approach:
Fix 1 — one shared builder, seven callers. Add linkScheduleUpdate(id, scheduleId) and unlinkScheduleUpdate(id) to the EXISTING desktop-client/src/util/schedule-actions.ts, each returning the pair with schedule_occurrence: null. All seven sites call one of them. Params typed string, NOT string | undefined. The two producers that today declare `scheduleId?: string` keep that declaration and add a local null guard instead of narrowing, so ScheduleEditForm.tsx needs NO edit.

Fix 2 — addTransfer derives the stamp once, next to matchedSchedule (transfer.ts:73): const matchedOccurrence = matchedSchedule === transaction.schedule ? transaction.schedule_occurrence : undefined. Use it in both writes. Mirror insert: put schedule_occurrence AFTER the ...transferTransaction spread alongside schedule (the literal at :61-71 already carries it and would otherwise win); undefined is dropped by skipNull and falls back to DEFAULT NULL. Main-leg update: explicit ?? null, load-bearing because convertForUpdate passes no options so a dropped key never reaches update()'s Object.keys(params) loop and the column would PRESERVE the old stamp.

Fix 3 — reword the comment at transfer.ts:133-136 to the real contract.

Fix 4 — keep transfer.test.ts:361-388 and relabel it a GUARD rather than deleting it; add one more labelled guard through batchUpdateTransactions and one genuinely discriminating relink case.

Fix 5 — the browser steps are staged so each discriminates, and each now carries its own op precondition. A Schedules-page Repeats-OFF schedule carries date op 'isapprox' and posts_transaction false, so getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate falls through to subDays(occurrenceDate, 2). QA Sch B dated 5 days out has a window starting today+3 (payment dated today sits outside) so it reads Paid BEFORE the fix and must NOT after. QA Sch C dated tomorrow has a window starting today-1 (payment inside, with a day of margin) so it reads not-Paid before and Paid after. Both steps first assert the rule's date condition reads `date is approx <date>`, because under op 'is' the window collapses onto the occurrence date and both steps would stop discriminating — the assertion the recorded rejection asked for.

acceptance.how_to_verify: qa_script steps 1-9; the discriminating read is QA Sch B's status cell. DERIVATION: B is created through the Schedules page with Repeats OFF, so its date condition's op is 'isapprox', not 'is' — ScheduleEditModal.tsx:76 seeds the initial condition as isapprox and schedule-edit-utils.ts:49 calls updateCond(conds.date, 'isapprox', 'date', fields.date), updateCond returns { ...cond, value } for an existing cond (:28-30) so the seeded op is preserved — and posts_transaction is seeded false (:75). getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate (shared/schedules.ts:90-102) therefore falls through both early returns and returns subDays(B.next_date, 2) = today+3, NOT the occurrence date. Before the fix the surviving stamp equals B.next_date (today+5), so arm 1 (:206) matches and B reads Paid; after, the stamp is null and arm 2 (:208-219) requires date >= today+3, which a payment dated today fails. The arithmetic is restated inline in qa_script steps 3 and 4 because the previous round got it wrong ('the occurrence date itself') and a tester reading only 'Repeats OFF' cannot tell which op the rule carries. Do not try to read schedule_occurrence off the transaction — it is rendered nowhere in the product.

qa_script: Open the app and click 'View demo' to load a synthetic budget.
Go to Schedules and add 'QA Sch A' — payee 'QA Payee A', account HSBC, 44.00, Repeats ON, starting 5 days from today.

Add 'QA Sch B' — payee 'QA Payee B', same account, same amount, Repeats OFF, date set to the SAME day as QA Sch A's next occurrence (5 days out). BEFORE MOVING ON, open QA Sch B's rule (Edit rule) and ASSERT its date condition reads `date is approx <date>` — NOT `date is <date>`. If it reads `is`, STOP: the derivation this step depends on does not hold. The shared occurrence date is the other half of the point: it is what makes the stale stamp equal B.next_date, which is what makes step 9 discriminate. Arithmetic to check against the rule in front of you: op 'isapprox' + posts_transaction OFF means getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate falls through to subDays(next_date, 2), so B's window starts at today+3 — not at today+5.

Add 'QA Sch C' — payee 'QA Payee C', same account, same amount, Repeats OFF, date set to TOMORROW. Apply the SAME assertion as step 3: open C's rule and confirm it reads `date is approx <tomorrow>`, not `date is <tomorrow>`; if it reads `is`, stop. C is used only by step 13. Its match window is occurrence-minus-2-days = today-1, so the payment dated today falls inside it with a day of margin. Under op `is` the window would instead be today+1, the payment dated today would fall OUTSIDE it, and step 13 would flip in the opposite direction and prove nothing.

Right-click QA Sch A and choose 'Post transaction today'. QA Sch A must now read Paid — paying an occurrence early is legitimate. The created row is dated TODAY but stamped with the occurrence 5 days out; that gap is the whole mechanism and every later step depends on this row never being re-dated.
Go to the HSBC register and find the QA Payee A row.
Hover the row, tick its select checkbox, click the '1 transactions' button and choose 'Unlink schedule'.
Return to Schedules: QA Sch A must read Upcoming again. This passes today too — it confirms the unlink landed, it does not detect the bug.

Back in the HSBC register, select the same row, choose 'Link schedule', pick QA Sch B. Return to Schedules and read QA Sch B's status cell. THIS IS THE DISCRIMINATING STEP for AC-1: before the fix it reads Paid — a schedule marked paid by another schedule's occurrence on a payment dated five days before it was due, because the surviving stamp today+5 equals B.next_date and arm 1 matches. After the fix the stamp is null, so only arm 2 can match and it requires date >= today+3, which a payment dated today fails. B must NOT read Paid. If B still reads Paid, first re-check the step 3 op assertion, then treat the fix as broken.
Confirm QA Sch A still reads Upcoming and that no unrelated schedule changed status.

Repeat steps 7-9 from the Schedules page instead of the register: open QA Sch A's edit page, select the transaction under 'Linked transactions', choose 'Unlink from schedule', then relink it to QA Sch B. B must again not read Paid. This covers the ScheduleEditModal site.
Repeat the unlink-and-relink from the mobile schedule page (narrow the viewport or use device emulation) to cover the third copy of the pair. The row must end linked to QA Sch B with no stamp.

With the QA Payee A row still linked to QA Sch B, unlink it from QA Sch B and then link it to QA Sch C — the row context action only offers 'Link schedule' while the row is unlinked, so both halves are required. QA Sch C MUST now read Paid. Why it reads Paid here and not in step 9: C's window starts at today-1 and the payment dated today is inside it, whereas B's window starts at today+3 and the same payment is outside it. Why this step discriminates: before the fix the surviving stamp (today+5) is neither C.next_date (today+1) nor null, so both arms fail and C reads not-Paid; after the fix the cleared stamp lets the date arm match and C reads Paid. This is the due to paid direction (AC-4).
risks: The fix clears the stamp on every relink, including a relink back to the schedule the row was already stamped for. Invisible whenever the payment's date is inside the new schedule's match window, but a payment dated more than 2 days before a recurring occurrence — or any date before a one-time schedule's date minus 2 days — loses its match on relink. QA step 13 probes the ordinary in-window case; the out-of-window case is the review risk and is deliberately untested.

The fix moves schedules from Due to Paid where a stale stamp was suppressing a legitimate match (AC-4). Correct, but the shape most likely to be mistaken for a regression, so it has its own criterion rather than being buried.

Both status-cell flips are derived from getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate's fallback branch and from getHasTransactionsQuery's two arms. The derivation was re-checked at every link, but nothing has been executed — node_modules is absent, so no test has run and the app has never started. The op assertion now in qa_script steps 3 and 4 exists because of exactly this class of failure: the previous round's derivation was wrong about the op and only review caught it. If a status cell does not flip as derived, check the rule's op before suspecting the fix.

The addTransfer fix is justified by the invariant and the verified insert/update asymmetry, not by a reproduction, and its production reachability is unproven: no UI-authored rule can set a schedule. If both writes are dead code in practice, Fix 2 is harmless but untested in production, at a cost of two lines.

Adding two exports to util/schedule-actions.ts means the new unit test imports a module that also pulls in the connection and query layers. If that bites in vitest, move the builders to a leaf module rather than mocking more of the tree.
The DiscoverSchedules site has no browser coverage and cannot get any: its input is server-side pattern matching over descriptions, not stageable by hand in a synthetic budget.
The mobile schedule edit page's link/unlink is changed but exercised by no automated test and only lightly in the QA script, which needs a narrow viewport to reach it at all.

@actual-app/api's updateTransaction surface, which can build the same stale-stamp diff because it diffs from a full-row read (api.ts:597). Not reachable from the UI.

Any change to getHasTransactionsQuery. Its two-arm shape is what makes the defect silent and what makes this fix's effect conditional on the payment's date.

RESOLVED BY RUNNING A COMPILER: packages/desktop-client/tsconfig.json:8 sets "strict": false while the root tsconfig.json:22 sets "strictFunctionTypes": true. The previous draft concluded from this that narrowing onLinkTransactions assigns fine, and carried ScheduleEditForm.tsx as a contingency. I built the same shape in isolation and ran tsc against it. The assignment compiles clean under `strictFunctionTypes: true, strict: false` — but the real reason is that `strict: false` also disables strictNullChecks, which is what makes `string | undefined` distinct from `string`; with it off, the optional and required signatures are the same type. The CONCLUSION (no ScheduleEditForm edit) holds, but the stated REASON was wrong: `strict: false` does not unset an explicitly-set `strictFunctionTypes`. The work order therefore does not rely on the flag at all — both producers keep their existing `scheduleId?: string` declarations and add a local null guard, so no other file's types change. ScheduleEditForm.tsx is dropped from files[] rather than carried as a contingency.

alternatives_considered.approach: Restage the rejected step 13 exactly as its two suggested branches: either post QA Sch B's OWN occurrence and confirm B reads Paid, or create a fresh register transaction dated on/after B's date and link that to B.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Both are non-discriminating, which is the point the rejection made. Posting B's own occurrence writes schedule and schedule_occurrence together through the server's own postTransactionForSchedule, which no client fix touches, so it reads Paid before and after. Linking a fresh in-window transaction never had a stamp, so the unlink defect cannot manifest. Either would have satisfied the objection's letter — a step that is TRUE on fixed code — while leaving the criterion with a guard that proves nothing. The third schedule is strictly better: it reuses the row that actually carries the stale stamp and puts it inside a window that genuinely contains the payment's date.

alternatives_considered.approach: Satisfy the recorded rejection by asserting the op only in prose in AC-1's how_to_verify, as the previous round already did, and leave qa_script steps 3 and 4 describing the schedules only as 'Repeats OFF, date set to <date>'.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is precisely what the rejection named as the defect. work_order.debate_summary:
There was no council to arbitrate. plan/critique.json is {} — the critic wrote nothing — and plan/proposal.json does not exist at all, so the proposer wrote nothing either. The only prior judgement is the recorded rejection of the earlier draft, whose single objection concerned qa_script step 13. I am reporting that plainly rather than implying a consensus nobody reached. Because nobody had attacked the plan, I re-derived its load-bearing claims from the source myself rather than accepting them: conform()'s insert/update asymmetry, db.update()'s per-key emission, all seven client write sites (a grep for `schedule_occurrence` across desktop-client/src returns test files only — no production write site exists, which is the defect in one line), transfer.ts's literal-plus-two-writes shape, getHasTransactionsQuery's two arms, getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate's fallback, the isapprox seeding preserved by updateCond, and postTransactionForSchedule's `date: today ? currentDay()`. All held.

What I changed. First and most important, I applied the recorded rejection, which was correct and had not been fully honoured. The previous round verified the isapprox chain in prose inside AC-1 and then left qa_script steps 3 and 4 describing the schedules only as 'Repeats OFF, date set to <date>'. Since qa_script is what the floor QA suite is generated from, a tester could not confirm the op, and under op `is` both status-cell flips would silently stop discriminating and pass for the wrong reason. Both steps now instruct the tester to open the schedule's rule and assert it reads `date is approx <date>` — not `date is <date>` — and to stop if it reads `is`; both carry their matchStartDate arithmetic restated inline. That is the rejection's required fix, applied where it asked for it rather than where it would have been easiest.

Second, I dropped ScheduleEditForm.tsx from the change. The previous round carried it as a contingency to be edited 'only if yarn typecheck requires it', which is a coin-flip, and it rested that coin on a misreading: it concluded that `strict: false` in desktop-client unsets the root's explicitly-set `strictFunctionTypes: true`. It does not — an explicitly-set flag survives a `strict` shorthand in either direction. I built the repo's exact shape in isolation and ran a real compiler against it. The conclusion survives anyway, but for a different reason: `strict: false` also disables strictNullChecks, which is what makes `string | undefined` distinct from `string`, so the optional and required signatures are the same type either way. Rather than leave the plan resting on a conclusion whose stated mechanism I had just shown to be wrong, I removed the dependency — both producers keep their existing `scheduleId?: string` declaration and add a local null guard, so no consumer's types change and the file leaves the PR. A file removed on evidence rather than carried as a hedge.

Third, I corrected the line numbers the previous round claimed to have corrected: it announced that MobileScheduleEditPage's pair 'sits at :139/:149, not :143/:151 as v4 stated', but :139 and :149 are the two function declarations and :143 and :151 the two payload lines — both v4's and its own citation were right about different things, and there was no mis-citation to correct. The work order names both pairs so no implementer has to guess.

What I did not change. I kept the relabelling of transfer.test.ts:361 rather than deletion — no production caller constructs its payload, and it is the only coverage of onUpdate propagating an explicit null to the mirror. I kept the addTransfer fix even though its production reachability is unproven (no UI-authored rule can set a schedule, so both writes may be dead code in practice); it is two lines, justified by the invariant and the verified insert/update asymmetry, and dropping it would leave the one server path that writes the schedule twice and the stamp zero times unfixed. I kept the fabrication fix: `source: IAC-1` through `IAC-7` is dropped from all seven criteria, because the issue body has no '## Acceptance (from the split)' section and the ledger's acceptance array is empty — a fabricated source is worse than none, since it asserts traceability to a split that does not exist. That also resolves the arbiter's split-criteria obligation: there are no IAC-n criteria to satisfy or defer. I kept stating plainly that a green suite is not evidence this change works: three CI cases and two browser steps discriminate, and everything labelled GUARD passes with the whole fix reverted.

Confidence 80, unchanged. Not raised, because the evidence I gathered confirms the previous round rather than adding to it, and the one genuinely new thing I did — compiling the tsconfig question — removed a hedge rather than adding certainty about the behaviour under test. Not lowered, because I found no load-bearing error: the two changes are a missing QA assertion and a contingent file, and the mis-citation I found was in the plan's commentary about itself, not in the instructions. It stays at 80 because nothing has been executed. node_modules is absent, so no test in this plan has ever run, the app has never started, and both status-cell flips are derived from the query's two arms rather than observed — and the previous round's derived step was exactly the thing that was wrong, which is why the op assertion now sits in the script instead of only in a rationale field. That number is load-bearing and I am not going to inflate it past what has actually been checked.
residual_risks: Rows already corrupt in a user's budget stay corrupt. Nothing repairs them; a stale stamp on an existing row can still suppress a legitimate occurrence match, the due to paid direction. This is the gap QA should understand before signing off, and the reason a follow-up migration is the natural next ticket.

The api package's updateTransaction can still build a diff that links a row to a new schedule while carrying the old stamp, because it diffs from a full-row read (api.ts:597). Not reachable from the UI, so not fixed here.

The transfer finding's 'both legs' claim is verified only by loot-core tests. No browser step can read a stamp — schedule_occurrence is rendered nowhere in the product — so QA cannot confirm it, and a reviewer should not read the QA script's green as covering it.

The addTransfer fix is verified by derivation and by the insert/update asymmetry, not by a reproduction, and its production reachability is unproven. If both writes are dead code in practice, Fix 2 is harmless but untested in production, at a cost of two lines.

The DiscoverSchedules auto-link site is covered by reading its payload shape and by sharing the tested builder. It has no browser coverage and cannot get any, because its input is server-side pattern matching that cannot be staged in a synthetic budget.
The mobile schedule edit page's link/unlink is changed but exercised by no automated test and only lightly in the QA script.

Both status-cell flips are derived from getHasTransactionsQuery's two arms, not observed in a running app. The previous plan's step was exactly this kind of derived-and-wrong step and was caught only in review. The op assertion in steps 3 and 4 narrows the way that step can be wrong, but does not eliminate it: if a status cell does not flip as derived, check the rule's op and the date the tester actually entered before suspecting the fix.

Any case labelled GUARD passes with the whole fix reverted. A green suite after this change is not evidence that this change works — the three discriminating CI cases plus the two discriminating browser steps are, and they are the ones to watch.

The three discriminating tests have never been executed. The two builder assertions are trivial and should settle on first run; the renderHook test and the addTransfer relink fixture are the two places implementation is most likely to need iteration.
